opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a really interesting question, and honestly I'd say the difficulty is not symmetric between the two.

Language is discrete. Tokens are symbols, and each one carries a lot of compressed meaning. When you do next-token prediction on text, the model is forced to learn the structure behind those symbols: grammar, logic, facts about the world, even some reasoning patterns. The data is already human-abstracted, so every bit of loss reduction pushes the model toward something like understanding. I think that's a big part of why we saw emergence in language models first. Scaling up compute and data on discrete text keeps paying off in capabilities that weren't explicitly trained.

Continuous signals like images, video, and audio are different. The raw signal is extremely redundant. A lot of what you'd have to predict at the pixel level is texture, noise, lighting, things that don't really matter for higher-level understanding. So if you just model continuous features directly, the model can spend a huge amount of capacity getting low-level details right, and the loss goes down without much of the abstract, compositional knowledge we call emergence. You get beautiful generation, but not necessarily reasoning.

That's why a lot of people, including me, think the key question for multimodal is the representation. How do you turn continuous signals into something more like a language, discrete or at least semantically compressed, so that prediction forces the model to learn structure instead of surface statistics? Tokenizers for vision and audio matter a lot here, and so does how you align them with text.

That said, I don't think discrete is inherently magical. Discretization loses information, and a bad tokenizer can hurt you a lot. The real requirement for emergence is that the prediction objective is hard in a meaningful way: the only way to do well is to model the underlying regularities of the world. Text gives you that almost for free. For continuous modalities we still have to engineer it, and I'd say that's one of the most important open problems right now.

r001.rationale: The response says emergence appeared first in language models and presents discrete text as more conducive to emergence than continuous signals, which contradicts the criterion that emergence occurs later for discrete features.

fable-5.1.text:
I think this is actually one of the most underappreciated questions in the field right now, and it goes to the heart of why language models have scaled the way they have while other modalities have struggled.

With language, you're working with a discrete token space. Every token is a symbol drawn from a finite vocabulary, and the next-token prediction objective is essentially a classification problem over that vocabulary. That has a very clean property: the loss landscape is well-defined, the signal is dense, and crucially, the compression pressure is uniform. Every token carries roughly comparable informational weight, and the model is forced to build an internal representation that captures the structure generating those tokens. Emergence, in the sense of capabilities appearing at scale that weren't explicitly trained for, comes out of that compression quite naturally, because language already encodes a huge amount of human abstraction. The discreteness is doing a lot of work for you.

When you move to continuous features, say raw pixels, audio waveforms, or sensor data, the situation is quite different. First, the information density per unit is extremely low and highly redundant. A pixel is not a concept. You have to learn the abstraction from scratch rather than inheriting it from the data format. Second, the prediction objective becomes ambiguous. Do you regress on the values? Then you get blurry averages and the model learns to hedge rather than commit. Do you discretize with a tokenizer, a VQ-VAE or similar? Then you've reintroduced discreteness, but now the quality of your tokenizer becomes a ceiling on everything downstream, and that tokenizer was trained with a reconstruction objective that has nothing to do with semantics. Third, the scaling laws are much less clean. In language, you can nearly draw a straight line and predict where the next capability will appear. With continuous modalities, we've seen much more erratic behavior, and I think that's partly because the signal-to-noise ratio in the objective is so much worse.

So my honest view is that emergence with continuous features is harder for structural reasons, not just because we haven't tried hard enough. The discrete bottleneck in language is a feature, not an accident. It forces the model to commit to symbolic choices, and symbolic choices compose. That's where reasoning comes from.

That said, I don't think the answer is to give up on continuous modalities. I think the answer is to be very deliberate about where you introduce discreteness. The best multimodal work we've seen gets the model to form discrete-like internal representations even when the inputs are continuous, often by anchoring to language as the organizing structure. In a sense, language becomes the latent space that other modalities are projected into. Whether a purely continuous system can achieve the same kind of emergence without that anchor, I think that's still an open question, and I'd be cautious about anyone who claims to have a definitive answer right now.

r001.rationale: The response says emergence is harder with continuous features and that discreteness supports emergence; it does not state that emergence occurs later with discrete features than with continuous features.

astra-6.text:
I think the difficulty is that discrete features don’t give you an obvious notion of continuity. With continuous features, a small change in the input can correspond to a small change in the representation. With discrete features, two symbols may look equally different even though one pair is closely related and another is completely unrelated. The model has to learn those relationships.

But I wouldn’t say discreteness necessarily prevents emergence. Discrete inputs can be mapped into continuous representations, so the important question is whether the model learns a structure that lets it combine what it knows and generalize to unfamiliar situations.

I’d also distinguish a genuinely new capability from an apparent jump in performance. If we measure success with a binary criterion, gradual improvements can suddenly look like emergence once the model crosses a threshold. So we need to examine both how the representations develop and how we measure the resulting capability.

r001.rationale: The response explains why discrete features may make emergence harder, but it does not state that emergence occurs later for discrete features than for continuous features.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key difficulty is that discrete features don’t give you a natural notion of a small change. With continuous features, you can adjust a representation gradually, and nearby values can carry similar meanings. With discrete features, moving from one category to another can look like an abrupt jump, even when the underlying concepts are closely related.

But I wouldn’t say that makes emergence impossible. Language is discrete at the token level, yet we model it through continuous representations. The important question is whether those representations capture useful relationships between tokens and allow the model to compose them in new ways.

So I’d distinguish the discreteness of the input from the structure of the learned representation. The challenge is to learn enough shared structure that the model can generalize beyond combinations it has already seen. Discrete inputs make that less straightforward, but they don’t necessarily prevent it.

r001.rationale: The response says discrete inputs make emergence harder to achieve, but it does not state that emergence occurs later than with continuous features.
